title: A motion designer’s showreel
description: Fifteen seconds of kinetic type, shifting shapes and tightly timed motion, rendered with Remotion.
inputs: A coding workspace with Remotion available. The shared prompt does not specify brand assets or audio.
steps: Copy the creator’s prompt into your coding agent and specify that the output should use Remotion.
Preview the composition and refine timing, typography and transitions before rendering.
Render an MP4 with Remotion. The creator’s result is a reference, not a guaranteed one-prompt output.
note: The author confirmed Remotion as the renderer. The short prompt leaves much of the art direction to the agent.

title: One shape. A whole interface.
description: A button becomes a player, a slider and a chart in one continuous, beat-driven loop.
inputs: 8–12 UI states, a palette, and music you have permission to use. The prompt also calls for Playwright, NumPy and FFmpeg.
steps: Choose your UI states, colors and audio before starting. The prompt asks the agent to confirm these inputs.
Review the beat grid and render still frames before committing to the full animation.
Use the requested Playwright and FFmpeg workflow to render the loop; check that the first and last frames connect.
note: This is a multi-tool workflow. Its rendering instructions are more involved than a single browser animation.

title: A little pixel magic
description: A spell-casting wizard, drawn and animated in a single HTML file. No external assets required.
inputs: A coding agent and a browser. The prompt explicitly requires no external assets, libraries or network requests.
steps: Copy the prompt into your coding agent and ask it to save the result as index.html.
Open the file in a browser. Check the idle, charge, cast and recovery animation states.
Adjust the palette or spell effect in a follow-up prompt, keeping the low-resolution pixel grid.
note: A useful first browser-animation exercise. The repository records the public prompt as a shared fragment.

title: Make derivatives visible
description: A visual introduction to derivatives, using Manim for the animation and edge-tts for narration.
inputs: A Python environment with Manim and edge-tts, plus any system dependencies required by those tools.
steps: Copy the prompt and specify the audience, lesson language and desired length.
Ask the agent to create a Manim scene and a narration script, then review the mathematical explanation.
Render the scene, generate narration with edge-tts and align the audio with the visual steps.
note: The original prompt is in Chinese; the text below is its English translation. The creator’s preview includes Chinese narration and text.

title: Your business, in five scenes
description: A 30-second explainer that moves from the customer’s problem to your offer, process and proof.
inputs: What you sell, who it is for, your brand colors, one proof point and your business name.
steps: Replace the bracketed business description in the prompt with your own information.
Ask the coding agent to save the animation as one HTML file, then preview it in a browser.
Review the five scenes and replace any unsupported claims. Exporting an MP4 requires a separate recording or rendering step.
note: The source identifies Claude Opus without confirming a version. This prompt produces a web animation; it does not specify an MP4 export workflow.

title: Follow a photon from the Sun
description: A storybook-style science explainer, with code-rendered visuals, narration and a little personality.
inputs: An environment for JavaScript animation and rendering, plus access to narration and audio tools. The prompt leaves the specific audio tools open.
steps: Read the full brief and decide which narration, music and rendering tools are available in your workspace.
Review the script and scientific estimates before rendering. Keep uncertainty visible in the explanation.
Build the scenes, review still frames, and check captions and audio timing in the final export.
note: This is an ambitious production brief. Tool access and follow-up work affect how much can be completed in one run.

title: Step inside a Starry Night
description: An explorable Van Gogh-inspired town, with twelve cats waiting to be found.
inputs: A Claude Code workspace and a browser. The creator noted that previous workspace context may have influenced the result.
steps: Copy the creator’s prompt into a coding workspace and ask for a browser-based 3D project.
Agree on movement controls, the visual direction and a small playable scene before expanding the town.
Run the project locally and test movement, object placement and cat discovery in your browser.
note: The original short prompt is available, but the author’s prior workspace context is not. The source does not confirm a specific 3D rendering library.

title: A world made for wandering
description: Monumental architecture, distant mountains and surreal ruins in an explorable browser landscape.
inputs: A coding workspace and a browser capable of running your chosen 3D renderer. The original source does not specify the renderer.
steps: Copy the prompt and choose a browser-based rendering library with your coding agent.
Start with terrain, one landmark and camera movement; review scale and composition.
Add environmental detail gradually and check performance while moving through the scene.
note: The author reported a substantial build session. The shared prompt alone does not describe every production step.

title: Market Street, before the earthquake
description: A historical reconstruction of San Francisco in 1906, assembled in Blender from documented sources.
inputs: Blender and historical reference sources, including maps, period photographs and film. The prompt asks the agent to research these before modeling.
steps: Build the historical source file requested by the prompt, recording evidence and uncertainty for each building.
Have the agent write Blender Python generators and assemble the scene from the documented data.
Inspect landmarks and camera movement before rendering the requested ten-second street journey.
note: Historical research is part of this task. A plausible-looking scene is not evidence of historical accuracy.
